---
title: "How our pipelines compare to community conventions"
subtitle: "Field guide"
description: "The Snakemake workflow catalog's standard layout next to the lab's, what we do differently, and which differences are worth keeping."
---

The Snakemake community has a recommended way to lay out a workflow, and the
[Snakemake workflow catalog](https://snakemake.github.io/snakemake-workflow-catalog/) lists
workflows that follow it. The lab's three pipelines follow a different pattern, inherited from
the PhanstielLab pipelines (dietJuicer, bagPipes). Neither is wrong. This page puts them side by
side so that when you read a catalog workflow, or someone reads ours, nothing is a surprise, and so
you know which of our habits are deliberate and which are just history.

## The two layouts {#layouts}

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Community layout

```
my-workflow/
├── workflow/
│   ├── Snakefile
│   ├── rules/          align.smk  peaks.smk ...
│   ├── envs/           *.yaml
│   ├── scripts/        *.py  *.R
│   ├── schemas/        config.schema.yaml  samples.schema.yaml
│   └── report/         captions for report()
├── config/
│   ├── config.yaml
│   ├── samples.tsv
│   └── README.md       how to configure (the catalog shows this)
├── .test/              tiny real data + config for CI
├── resources/          downloaded references
└── results/            everything the workflow writes
```

You run it with `snakemake --cores 8 --sdm conda` from the repository root (Snakemake finds
`workflow/Snakefile` on its own), and a cluster profile lives with the user, not the workflow.

## Lab layout

```
MicroCPipe/
├── MicroCPipe.sh  MicroCMerge.sh  unlock.sh     # launchers
├── MicroCSamplesheet.txt
├── config/        MicroCConfig.yaml  requirements.txt
├── profiles/      local  longleaf  pioneer  biowulf  slurm-template
│                  (each: config.yaml + env.sh)
├── workflows/     MicroCPipe.snakefile  MicroCMerge.snakefile
│                  rules/common.smk  rules/formats.smk
├── envs/          microc_*.yml
├── scripts/       get_qc.py  qc_report.py ...
├── tests/         test_dryrun.py  dryrun/ (fixture)
└── docs/          Quarto site
```

You run it with `bash MicroCPipe.sh` or `sbatch MicroCPipe.sh`. Outputs go to `output/` (or
`outputDir`).

:::

## Side by side {#table}

| Topic | Community convention | Lab pipelines | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entry point | `workflow/Snakefile`, found automatically | `workflows/<Name>.snakefile`, always passed with `-s` | Cosmetic. Keep, but see below |
| Rule files | `workflow/rules/*.smk` | `workflows/rules/*.smk` (MicroCPipe, TTpipe); one file (ChromSimPipe) | Same idea |
| Config | `config/config.yaml` | `config/<Name>Config.yaml` | Same idea |
| Samplesheet | `config/samples.tsv` | `<Name>Samplesheet.txt` at the root | Same idea |
| Config validation | `validate(config, "schemas/config.schema.yaml")` | Hand-written checks in Python at parse time | Worth adding a schema |
| Outputs | `results/`, `resources/`, `logs/` | Everything under `outputDir` (default `output/`), logs inside it | Deliberate, keep |
| Profiles | With the user (`~/.config/snakemake/`) or `workflow/profiles/default` | `profiles/<site>/` in the repository, one per cluster | Deliberate, keep |
| Resources | `threads:` and often `resources:` in rules | Only `threads:` in rules; memory, time and partition in profiles | Deliberate, but restructure |
| Launch | `snakemake ...` directly | Launcher script that is itself a SLURM job | Deliberate, keep |
| Snakemake install | conda/mamba environment | pip into a venv (`env/`) made by the launcher | Deliberate, keep |
| Tool installs | `conda:` per rule, or wrappers | `conda:` per rule; no wrappers | Fine |
| Reports | `report()` + `snakemake --report` | Own static HTML dashboards | Fine |
| Reuse | `module` + `use rule * from ...` | `include:` with a hook function (MicroCPipe) | Fine at this size |
| Linting | `snakemake --lint` and snakefmt in CI | Not run | Worth adding |
| Tests | `.test/` with tiny real data, a real run in CI | pytest dry runs on placeholder fixtures (MicroCPipe, TTpipe); unit tests only (ChromSimPipe) | Different, both useful |

## What we do differently, and why {#differences}

### `workflows/*.snakefile` instead of `workflow/Snakefile` {#entry-point}

MicroCPipe has two workflows (core and merge) in one repository, so it needs two names, and the
launchers always pass `-s`. The cost is small but real: `snakemake -n` in the repository root does
nothing useful, editors do not recognize `.snakefile` as Snakemake without a setting, and the
catalog's tools look for `workflow/Snakefile`. Renaming the folder to `workflow/` and the main file to
`Snakefile` (keeping `merge.smk` or a second Snakefile beside it) would cost one line in each launcher.
Low priority.

### Profiles in the repository {#profiles}

The catalog treats the cluster as the user's business. The lab ships one profile per cluster
because the people running the pipelines move between a few known clusters, and a profile that
already has the right partition names saves each of them a day. The launchers pick the profile from
`--profile`, then `$<NAME>_PROFILE`, then `hpcProfile` in the config, so the repository stays
neutral and each person sets their cluster once in `~/.bashrc`. Keep this. Two things to fix:

- Shipped profiles should not contain real account names. MicroCPipe and TTpipe use `<account>`
  placeholders and MicroCPipe's launcher refuses to start until they are filled in; ChromSimPipe's
  `longleaf` and `pioneer` profiles carry real accounts.
- Snakemake 8 automatically uses `profiles/default/` (relative to the current directory, then to
  the Snakefile) as a *workflow profile*. The lab's `profiles/` folder is exactly where Snakemake
  looks, so never name a site profile `default` unless you mean that.

### Resources only in profiles {#resources}

Rules declare `threads:` and nothing else; `set-threads` and `set-resources` in each profile give
every rule its CPUs, memory and time. This is the dietJuicer pattern, and it is a good one: moving to
a new cluster never touches a rule, and the numbers sit next to the partition names they depend on.

The problem is duplication. MicroCPipe's five profiles repeat the same 16 `set-threads` lines and
the same `set-resources` block, and TTpipe's repeat 24 rules. Add a rule and you edit five files;
forget one and that rule silently gets `default-resources` on that cluster. This has already
happened: TTpipe's eight spike-in rules appear in none of its profiles. The `threads:` in each
rule is also overridden by every profile, so the same number lives in six places.

Snakemake 8 has a direct fix. It reads two profiles: the general one (`--profile`) and a workflow
profile (`--workflow-profile`, default `profiles/default/`). Settings in the workflow profile
override the general one. So:

- `profiles/default/config.yaml`: `set-threads` and `set-resources` for every rule, once.
- `profiles/<site>/config.yaml`: `executor`, `jobs`, `latency-wait`, `default-resources` with the
  account and partition, and the GPU partition for the one rule that needs it.

A site that needs a bigger number for one rule (a cluster with large-memory nodes) can still pass
`--set-resources hic:mem_mb=200000` from its launcher call or keep its own override. This keeps the
lab's idea (no resources in rules) and removes the copies.

### A launcher script {#launcher}

Catalog workflows are started with `snakemake` directly. The lab's launchers do four things a bare
command does not: they are themselves a small SLURM job (`#SBATCH -t 10-00:00:00`), so the
Snakemake process survives you logging out; they pick the site profile; they create the Snakemake
venv if needed; and they always add `--rerun-incomplete --keep-going -p` and the SLURM log
directory. For people who run one pipeline a few times a year, that is worth a lot. Keep it.

The cost is that the three launchers are copies of one idea, and they have drifted:

| | MicroCPipe.sh | TTpipe.sh | ChromSimPipe.sh |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activates the venv | no (on purpose, see [MicroCPipe](microcpipe.qmd#mc-launcher)) | yes | yes |
| Stops on an unedited `<placeholder>` | yes | no | no |
| Checks that `env.sh` exists | yes | yes | no |
| `cores: 100` in SLURM profiles | yes | no | no (uses `cpus_per_task`) |

MicroCPipe's version is the most careful. Bringing the other two up to it is the
cheapest improvement on this page.

### Snakemake from pip, in a venv {#venv}

The catalog's instructions install Snakemake with conda or mamba. The lab installs it with pip
(`snakemake==8.27.1` in `config/requirements.txt`) into a venv the launcher builds. The reason is
in the profiles' `env.sh` files: the conda modules on the lab's clusters are older than Snakemake
8.27 accepts, so each person installs Miniforge for the per-rule environments anyway, and keeping
Snakemake itself out of conda means one less environment to solve. Pinning the exact Snakemake
version in a text file is also easy to read. Keep it, with two notes: the SLURM executor plugin is
not pinned (`>=1.0` in two repositories, unpinned in ChromSimPipe), and the launcher runs `pip
install` on every start, which needs network access on the node the launcher runs on.

### Hand-written validation instead of schemas {#validation}

Catalog workflows call `validate(config, "schemas/config.schema.yaml")` and
`validate(samples, "schemas/samples.schema.yaml")`. A JSON schema checks types, required keys and
allowed values, and can fill in defaults. The lab's pipelines check the config and samplesheet in
Python at parse time instead (TTpipe's `common.smk` and ChromSimPipe's `parameters.py` have dozens of
checks). Those checks do things a schema cannot, such as "`reference_condition` must be a
`Condition` in the samplesheet" or "the GTF and the genome use the same chromosome naming", and their
messages say how to fix the problem. A schema would still help with the simple cases and would
document every key in one file. Use both: a schema for types and allowed values, Python for the
checks that compare one input with another.

### No wrappers {#wrappers}

[Snakemake wrappers](https://snakemake-wrappers.readthedocs.io/) are tested, versioned snippets
for common tools (`wrapper: "v3.x.x/bio/samtools/sort"`). The lab writes the shell commands itself,
with pinned tools in `envs/*.yml`. For pipelines like MicroCPipe, where the exact flags *are* the
method (`bwa mem -5SP -T0`, the pairtools options), a visible shell command is easier to review and
cite than a wrapper call. Fine as is.

### Own HTML reports instead of `report()` {#reports}

Snakemake's `report()` flag marks outputs for `snakemake --report report.html`, which bundles
them with run statistics and the workflow graph. The lab writes its own static dashboards
(`qc_report.py` in MicroCPipe and TTpipe) with thresholds from the config. Those do more than
`--report` would. Snakemake's between-workflow cache (`cache: True` on a rule, with
`--cache`) is a different feature that would suit expensive reference steps, such as TTpipe's
`star_index`, if several projects share one index. Not needed today.

### `include:` with a hook instead of `module` {#modules}

MicroCPipe's `formats.smk` is included by two Snakefiles, each defining `get_pairs()` first (see
[MicroCPipe](microcpipe.qmd#mc-include)). Snakemake's module system (`module formats: snakefile:
...` then `use rule cool from formats with: input: ...`) does the same with an explicit interface, and
also lets another lab reuse our rules without copying them. For two Snakefiles in one repository,
`include:` is simpler to read. Switch only if the format rules start being reused across
repositories.

## What `snakemake --lint` says {#lint}

We ran `snakemake --lint` (Snakemake 8.27.1) from each pipeline's root at the pinned commits. MicroCPipe
and TTpipe were given their dry-run test configs so they parse without data; ChromSimPipe parses
with its shipped config, because linting does not build the job graph and so does not need the
input files. All three exit with status 1 (lints found).

<!-- GENERATE: microcpipe-lint | pipelines/microcpipe | snakemake --lint -s workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile --configfile config/MicroCConfig.yaml tests/dryrun/config.yaml -->
<!-- GENERATE: ttpipe-lint | pipelines/ttpipe | snakemake --lint -s workflows/TTpipe.snakefile --configfile config/TTpipeConfig.yaml tests/dryrun/config.yaml -->
<!-- GENERATE: chromsimpipe-lint | pipelines/chromsimpipe | snakemake --lint -s workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile -->

| Lint | MicroCPipe | TTpipe | ChromSimPipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Absolute path | 40 | 151 | 0 |
| Path composition with `+` | 34 | 131 | 0 |
| Mixed rules and functions in same snakefile | 1 | 5 | 1 |
| Shell command uses a variable from outside the rule | 0 | 8 (`PY` 4, `SCRIPTS` 4) | 0 |
| Param is a prefix of an input or output but hardcoded | 0 | 6 | 0 |
| No log directive | 0 | 1 (`sample_table`) | 0 |
| Long `run:` block, move to a script | 0 | 1 (`sample_table`) | 0 |
| Environment variable used without `envvars:` | 0 | 0 | 1 (`CHROMSIM_CONFIG`) |

How to read this:

- **"Absolute path" and "path composition" are one issue, and mostly a false alarm.** Rules
  write `OUT + "/{group}/logs/..."`. The linter sees a string that starts with `/` and calls it
  absolute; it also dislikes building paths with `+`. `OUT` comes from the config, so nothing is
  really hard-coded. ChromSimPipe writes the same paths as f-strings
  (`f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/..."`) and gets neither lint. Switching to f-strings would remove 356 of
  the 380 findings across the three pipelines and make the rest easy to see.
- **Shell variables from outside the rule** (`{PY}`, `{SCRIPTS}` in TTpipe) work, because
  Snakemake fills shell placeholders from global variables too, but a reader cannot see them in the
  rule. Pass them as `params:`.
- **Hardcoded param prefixes** are params like `outdir = OUT + "/qc/fastqc"` that repeat part of an
  output path. If the output moves, the param does not. Deriving it from the output
  (`lambda w, output: os.path.dirname(output.zip)`) keeps them in step.
- **`sample_table`** is the only `run:` block and the only rule without a log. Both lints are fair
  and both are small.
- **`envvars:`** is half right for ChromSimPipe: the Snakefile *sets* `CHROMSIM_CONFIG` rather than
  reading it, so asserting it would not help. The lint does point at something real, though: the
  scripts depend on environment variables that Snakemake does not track.
- **Mixed rules and functions**: the linter wants helper functions in `common.smk`. MicroCPipe and
  TTpipe mostly do this already; the remaining functions sit next to the one rule that uses them,
  which we think reads better.
- In our run, the line numbers the linter gave for rules in included `.smk` files did not match the
  files. Find the rule by name.
- Linting ChromSimPipe runs its parse-time code, which writes
  `output/<run name>_ChromSimSamplesheet.txt` (see [ChromSimPipe](chromsimpipe.qmd#cs-parse-time)).

Nothing in the lint output is a bug. The linter does not catch the things that matter most in
these pipelines, such as the stale-samplesheet bug TTpipe fixed or ChromSimPipe's parameters that
Snakemake cannot see. Run it anyway: once the false alarms are gone, it is a cheap CI step that
catches new habits creeping in.

## Tests: dry runs versus `.test/` {#tests}

Catalog workflows usually ship a `.test/` folder with a few thousand real reads and run the whole
workflow in CI. MicroCPipe and TTpipe instead run `snakemake -n` against placeholder files and
assert job counts (see [TTpipe](ttpipe.qmd#tt-tests)). Dry runs are fast, need no conda
environments, and are very good at catching broken wiring, switches that pull in the wrong rules,
and samplesheet parsing. They cannot catch a wrong flag or a tool that crashes. A small real-data
run catches those, but takes minutes and needs the environments. The two are complements. For
ChromSimPipe, which has neither, a dry-run fixture is the first thing to add; a real run in CI is
not possible without a GPU.

## What is worth changing, in order {#ranked}

1. **Bring TTpipe's and ChromSimPipe's launchers up to MicroCPipe's** (no venv activation,
   placeholder check, `env.sh` check) and add `cores: 100` where rules use `threads:`.
2. **Remove real account names from ChromSimPipe's shipped profiles.**
3. **Move per-rule `set-threads`/`set-resources` into one workflow profile** (`profiles/default/`)
   and keep only site settings in `profiles/<site>/`.
4. **Add a dry-run fixture and CI to ChromSimPipe.**
5. **Write paths as f-strings and add `snakemake --lint` to CI.**
6. **Add JSON schemas** for the configs and samplesheets, keeping the cross-checks in Python.
7. **Rename `workflows/` to `workflow/`** if the pipelines ever go into the catalog.

Everything else on this page (launchers, profiles in the repository, pip-installed Snakemake, own
reports, shell commands instead of wrappers, outputs under one folder) is a deliberate choice that
suits how the lab works.
